Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on modern warfare continues with another video on the Russian Invasion of Ukraine with the updates of February 2026. Four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Ukraine is still standing and still fighting back. In this latest Ukraine war update, we examine how battlefield conditions evolved in February, from Russia’s growing reliance on infiltration tactics to the sudden disruption caused by the disabling of unauthorized Starlink terminals. That communications breakdown opened the door for a series of Ukrainian clearing operations in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, allowing Kyiv to retake territory and stabilize several threatened sectors. The video also tracks the wider battlefield, where Russia continues pressing in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, Sloviansk, and Lyman directions while maintaining missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. On the diplomatic front, we cover Ukraine’s expanding domestic arms production, new Western military aid packages, and the uncertain state of negotiations involving Kyiv, Moscow, Europe, and the United States. Finally, the episode closes with a strategic summary of the war’s current trajectory and a comparison of visually confirmed equipment losses suffered by both sides. This is a clear and detailed overview of where the Russia-Ukraine war stands now, what changed in February, and what may come next on the battlefield and in diplomacy.

The Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on medieval history continues with a coverage of the Catalan Company. Mercenaries are supposed to fight for coin, not carve out kingdoms—but the Great Catalan Company did both. Born from Aragonese and Sicilian veterans of the War of the Sicilian Vespers, these fearsome light infantrymen—the Almogavars—sailed east into a shattered Mediterranean shaped by the Fourth Crusade, Latin principalities, and Turkic beyliks gnawing at Byzantine Anatolia. Hired by Emperor Andronikos II after the disaster at Bapheus, Roger de Flor’s company arrives in Constantinople, clashes violently with Genoese rivals, and is rushed into Asia Minor. There the Catalans win battles, lift sieges, and terrorize the countryside with shock tactics, sparks on steel, and brutal plunder that turns their “allies” into enemies. In 1305 a palace plot kills Roger at Adrianople—triggering a bloody Catalan vengeance from Gallipoli across Thrace and Macedonia. Leadership feuds follow, but the company’s luck returns in Greece: after being shortchanged, they destroy the Duke of Athens at Halmyros (1311) and seize Athens and Thebes. The video traces their rule, pragmatic alliances with Venice and even former Turkic foes, and their slow decline as Florentine and Navarrese adventurers dismantle Catalan power. By the end, you’ll see why “Catalan” became an insult in parts of Greece—and why Barcelona, Palermo, and Athens share a hidden medieval story.

Kings and Generals historical animated documentary series on the history of the early modern world and the Ottoman history continues with a video on the Origins of the Ottoman Army. In this opening episode of a new series on the history and evolution of the Ottoman military, we explore how a small frontier warrior society in Bithynia laid the foundations for one of the most powerful armies in world history. Beginning with the nomadic warfare traditions of Turkic tribes and the legacy of the Seljuks, the video traces how the Kayı tribe emerged in the unstable borderlands of northwestern Anatolia after the Mongol disruptions and Byzantine decline. The episode then follows Osman Gazi and the early Ottoman beylik, examining how the Ottomans combined steppe cavalry tactics, frontier raiding, local alliances, and political adaptability to defeat Byzantine forces and expand rapidly. It also highlights the role of the Ahis guilds, religious legitimacy, and cross-cultural cooperation with local Christian elites and mercenaries. Finally, the video explains the first major military reforms under Orhan and his successors: the creation of the Yaya and Müsellem corps and the development of the timar system, which transformed tribal cavalry into the Timarli Sipahi provincial force. These innovations gave the Ottomans a durable military structure and set the stage for the rise of the Janissaries in the next episode.

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on modern warfare continues with another video on the Russian Invasion of Ukraine with the updates of January 2026. This 2026 update on the Russia–Ukraine war examines how the conflict has entered its fourth year with no decisive breakthrough, despite enormous human and material costs. The video begins with a battlefield overview shaped by extreme winter conditions that have slowed advances but intensified localized fighting across Donbas, Kupiansk, Zaporizhia, and border sectors. Particular attention is given to creeping Russian offensives, contested urban strongpoints, and the strategic implications of potential pincer movements near Lyman and the broader fortress belt. A major focus is the escalating air campaign targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure through mass drone swarms and ballistic missiles, testing the limits of air defense capacity and contributing to blackouts, infrastructure damage, and civilian hardship during freezing temperatures. The diplomatic landscape is explored through two parallel tracks: limited strike moratoriums and shuttle negotiations on one side, and European-led security guarantee discussions on the other. The episode also reviews international military aid, new air defense systems, domestic Ukrainian arms production, and the evolving balance of external support. It concludes with a data-driven comparison of visually confirmed equipment losses for both sides, underscoring the scale of attrition and the central importance of air defense in shaping the war’s next phase.

all_videos.description:
🎥 Watch 250+ exclusive videos on ✔ youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and ✔ Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on modern warfare and naval warfare continues with a video on the Anglo-German naval race prior to the Great War. From Trafalgar’s legacy to the launch of HMS Dreadnought, this video breaks down how sea power shaped the modern world—and why Germany’s attempt to challenge Britain at sea helped push Europe toward catastrophe. We begin with the 19th-century revolution in warship technology: ironclads, steam propulsion, heavier guns, and the rise of the “pre-dreadnought” battleship. Then we meet the ideas that fueled the rivalry, especially Alfred Thayer Mahan’s argument that national greatness depended on decisive fleet battles and maritime supremacy. With Kaiser Wilhelm II determined to make Germany a world power, Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz arrives with his “risk theory”: build a fleet strong enough that Britain can’t win without crippling losses. The result is a sequence of Naval Laws that steadily expands Germany’s battleships and cruisers—until Britain responds with the Two-Power Standard, diplomatic realignment, and Admiral “Jacky” Fisher’s sweeping reforms. When Dreadnought launches, the race escalates into panic, propaganda, and political crisis, before attempted diplomacy fails and both powers march toward World War.

Kings and Generals historical animated documentary series on the history of Rome, Roman Empire and Ancient world continues with a video in which we wonder why did the Romans — master of the Mediterranean world — fail to conquer Germania? In this episode, we explore one of the most enduring questions of Roman history: why the legions that subdued Gaul, Hispania, Greece, and Egypt were repeatedly frustrated by the Germanic tribes beyond the Rhine. Drawing on ancient sources like Tacitus, alongside modern scholarship, this video examines the geographic, logistical, economic, military, and cultural factors that made Germania uniquely resistant to Roman conquest. 
From the hostile terrain and immense logistical costs of campaigning deep into forests and bogs, to the decentralized tribal structure that denied Rome decisive victories, Germania posed challenges unlike any other frontier. Catastrophic defeats such as the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest shattered Roman confidence and permanently altered imperial strategy, forcing Rome to abandon expansion in the north in favor of fortified borders and mobile defense. We also explore why Germania was seen as economically “not worth” conquering, how cultural and ideological differences hindered Romanisation, and why cooperation and alliance ultimately replaced conquest as Rome’s preferred approach. In the end, Germania was not conquered — it was contained, shaping the future of both Rome and Europe itself.

all_videos.description:
🎥 Watch 250+ exclusive videos on Youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals historical animated documentary series on the history of the early modern world, India and colonialism continues with a video on how the British India Company started the conquest of India. Previously we have covered the Rise of the British East India Company (https://youtu.be/_SHhiEISRrE). In the early 1700s, the East India Company—once a globe-trotting merchant venture known as “John Company”—began its transformation into a conquest machine. As the Mughal Empire weakened after Aurangzeb’s death and regional powers like the Marathas surged, India became a fragmented battleground ripe for intervention. The Company exploited this chaos by building a professional, corporate army: a small European core reinforced by vast numbers of sepoys, trained and equipped in European style. Next, the story shifts to the Carnatic Wars, where British and French trading companies fought proxy conflicts tied to wider European wars, and where Robert Clive emerged as a decisive figure. From the audacious seizure of Arcot to the crisis in Bengal, the Company’s path to dominance accelerates. The episode culminates in Plassey—depicted less as a battle and more as a political-financial transaction—followed by victories that secured revenue rights and real control over Bengal. Finally, the video examines the grim consequences of Company rule: corruption, extraction, scandal at home, and catastrophe in Bengal, setting the stage for the next conquests across India.

Kings and Generals historical animated documentary series on the history of Rome and Iran, continues with a video in which we talk about the rivalry between the Roman empire and the Parthian Kingdom. For nearly seven centuries, Rome and Persia stood as rival superpowers, locked in one of history’s longest and most complex geopolitical struggles. From the catastrophic Roman defeat at Carrhae to repeated invasions of Mesopotamia and the sackings of Ctesiphon, this rivalry shaped the political landscape of the ancient world. But why did Rome—so successful in Gaul, Spain, and the Mediterranean—fail to conquer Persia? And why did this frontier stabilize where it did? In this episode, we explore the Roman–Persian frontier not as a rigid border, but as a dynamic zone shaped by geography, logistics, economics, and diplomacy. Drawing on ancient authors and modern historians, we examine why traditional explanations of Roman “failure” fall short, and how concepts like periphery, client kingdoms, and supply networks defined the limits of imperial power. We also take a deep dive into Trajan’s eastern campaign, the economic realities of ancient warfare, and why capturing Persian capitals never translated into lasting conquest. Ultimately, Rome and Persia were not eternal enemies because they could not defeat each other—but because equilibrium was the most sustainable outcome for both empires.

all_videos.description:
🎥 Watch 250+ exclusive videos on ✔ youtube ► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join and ✔ Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals animated historical documentary series on modern warfare and naval warfare continues with a video on the evolution of the Dreadnought. For centuries, control of the seas defined global power. From towering sailing ships to steel leviathans driven by turbines, naval warfare evolved through relentless technological competition. This video traces the transformation of war at sea from the Age of Sail to the launch of HMS Dreadnought, the battleship that rendered every rival fleet obsolete overnight. We begin with the sailing ship of the line and the rise of broadside combat, before following the disruptive arrival of steam propulsion and explosive Paixhans shells. These innovations shattered wooden navies and led to ironclads, rotating turrets, and radically new ship designs. As gunnery, armor, and propulsion advanced together, navies settled into the pre-dreadnought formula—a balance of firepower, protection, and speed. Strategic thinking evolved alongside technology. Alfred Thayer Mahan’s theory of sea power reshaped naval doctrine, while Germany’s challenge to British dominance ignited a dangerous arms race. The lessons of the Russo-Japanese War finally pointed the way forward. In 1906, HMS Dreadnought combined all-big-gun armament, turbine propulsion, and unprecedented speed—redefining naval warfare and pushing the world toward industrialized conflict on an unprecedented scale.

Kings and Generals' historical animated documentary series on the history of Rome continues with the sixth episode of our coverage of the Second Punic War with Scipio's masterpiece - the Battle of Zama in 202 BC. Previously we have covered Hannibal's masterpiece - the battle of Cannae in 216 BC (https://youtu.be/gObVeaEzklM). In 202 BC, two of history’s greatest commanders finally faced one another on the plains of North Africa. Hannibal Barca, the terror of Rome and victor of Cannae, met Publius Cornelius Scipio, Rome’s rising star, in a confrontation that would decide the fate of the Mediterranean world. After sixteen years of brutal war, betrayals, and shattered armies, the Second Punic War reached its dramatic climax at Zama. Hannibal returned from Italy with his battle-hardened veterans, while Scipio arrived with a disciplined Roman army and powerful Numidian allies. Before the fighting began, the rivals met face to face in a tense parley—peace was offered, rejected, and fate sealed. This episode follows the final campaign step by step: Carthage’s failed armistice, the last diplomatic maneuvers, the march to Zama, and the clash of elephants, infantry, and cavalry. We break down the tactics, formations, and critical decisions that led to Rome’s ultimate victory—and Carthage’s irreversible decline. Witness how Scipio reversed Cannae, how Hannibal’s last gamble failed, and how one battle reshaped Roman dominance for centuries to come. This is the dramatic conclusion of the Second Punic War.
